title: Why We Still Need Each Other
subtitle: A five-session study on the church, the body of Christ, and the call to belong to a people who will let you down.
summary:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and anyone who has loved the church and been wounded by it in roughly equal measure, which is to say almost everyone who has stayed long enough to know what they are talking about. It walks slowly through five movements on what the church actually is, on the life together that Bonhoeffer described from inside a community that the state would soon scatter and kill, on the marks and the mess of a church that is a hospital of sinners and not a museum of saints, on the church sent into a culture that no longer assumes the faith, and on the hard grace of committing to a flawed people instead of leaving the moment they prove flawed. It is built to be run by a busy volunteer with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than a tidy resolution.

This is not a study that defends the church by pretending it is fine. It will not do that, and the leader must never let it. The church has covered up abuse, baptized politics, traded its prophets for its donors, and bored a watching world half to death. The study takes all of that seriously and refuses to flinch. But it also refuses the easy exit, the conviction common to the wounded that the answer to a hypocritical church is no church, that a Christian can follow Jesus alone with a podcast and a Bible app. The New Testament knows no such Christian. Bell writes as a working pastor who has watched the church fail up close, who has been the failure more than once, and who loves her anyway, the way you love a family you cannot disown because it is the only family there is. He does not stand outside this. He has been the hypocrite in the pulpit. He writes from inside the body. So will you.
audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

sessions.title: What the Church Actually Is
sessions.aim: To strip away the false pictures of the church as a building, an event, or a service we attend, and to recover the New Testament reality that the church is a people, the body of Christ, the called-out ones, so that the room sees why the Bible knows no solitary Christian.
sessions.summary: A man told Bell he loved Jesus but was finished with the church, that he could worship God just fine on a Saturday morning with his coffee and his Bible. Bell did not argue with him. He asked him a question instead. Where, in the whole New Testament, do you find a single Christian living like that. The first question is not whether the church has failed us. It plainly has. The first question is what the church even is, because most of us are angry at, or bored by, or done with a thing we have never correctly named. Bell takes the strong form of the two pictures that quietly run our imaginations. The first says the church is a building, a place you go, and it is right that the church gathers in places and that the gathering matters. The second says the church is an event, a service you attend and rate, music and a talk and a feeling, and it is right that we gather to worship and that what happens when we gather is not nothing. But neither picture is the thing. The church is not a building, which is why the New Testament writers never once use the word for one. The church is not an event, which is why Paul calls it a body and not a performance. The Greek word is ekklesia, the called-out assembly, a people summoned by God out of the world and bound to one another. You do not attend a body. You are a member of it, in the surgeon's sense, a limb that dies if it is severed. That is why there is no solitary Christian in the New Testament. Not because it is forbidden but because it is impossible, the way a hand is not a hand once it is cut off the arm.

keyScripture.why: Paul tells the Corinthians that they are the body of Christ and individually members of it, naming the church not as a place they go or an event they attend but as a single living body of which each of them is a part, so that to be a Christian alone is as strange as a severed hand.

discussion.q: Before tonight, when you heard the word church, what was the first picture in your mind, a building, a Sunday service, a denomination, or a group of people?
discussion.behind: Surface the working definition before correcting it. Most people in the room picture a building or an event, and that picture quietly shapes everything they feel about the church, including their grievances. The point is not to settle the answer yet but to expose the unexamined image. Land it on honesty, not the right answer. Go first if the room is slow.

discussion.q: Bell asks where in the New Testament you find a single Christian following Jesus alone, with no church. Why do you think the New Testament has no category for that?
discussion.behind: Move the room off the modern assumption that faith is private. The aim is to notice that the Bible does not argue against solitary Christianity so much as it cannot imagine it. Help them feel that the call to Christ in the New Testament is always, at the same time, a call into a people.

discussion.q: Paul calls the church a body and says each person is a member of it. What changes when you stop thinking of yourself as someone who attends a church and start thinking of yourself as a body part?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge image of the session. A member, in Paul's sense, is a limb, not a card-carrier. Help the room feel the difference between a consumer who attends and a hand that belongs. The point is that membership in the body is not a transaction but an organic fact, with all the dependence that implies.

discussion.q: Bell grants that the church gathers in buildings and that worship services matter. So what is lost when we let the building or the service become the whole of what we mean by church?
discussion.behind: Protect the even-handedness. The building is not nothing and the service is not nothing. The error is the shrinking, letting the place or the event swallow the people. Make sure the room does not leave thinking gatherings are unimportant. The error is mistaking the shell for the body inside it.

discussion.q: Bell admits he has spent whole seasons treating the church as a service he produced rather than a people he belonged to. Where have you treated the church as something you consume rather than something you are part of?
discussion.behind: Move from definition to self-implication. You are not hunting for confession to shame anyone, including yourself. You want each person, the leader first, inside the question, because the consumer instinct is in all of us, pastor and member alike. Go first, and name your own version of it plainly.

objections.objection: I can follow Jesus on my own. I do not need an organized church with all its hypocrisy and politics and disappointment. Me and God, a Bible, maybe a good podcast, that is the real thing, and the rest is just institution.
objections.response: Sit with what is true here, because there is something. The institution can be a barnacle on the body, and a great deal of what people call church really is just machinery, programs and budgets and politics that have little to do with Christ. The grievance against that is often righteous. Then make the distinction with care. What you are describing, you and God alone, is not found anywhere in the New Testament, not as a forbidden option but as an impossible one. When God saves a person he does not merely reconcile them to himself, he makes them part of a people, a body, a household, a temple built of living stones. The hand cannot say to the body I have no need of you and remain a hand. It becomes a dead thing. The Christian who walks away from all of it to follow Jesus alone has not found a purer faith. He has tried to be a limb without a body, and the New Testament does not know what that creature is.

objections.objection: The church is just a man-made institution that grew up over the centuries, an organization with leaders and money and power like any other. Calling it the body of Christ is just sacred language papered over an ordinary human club.
objections.response: Grant the part that is real, because the church is in fact a human institution and behaves like one, with all the failure that implies, and pretending otherwise is its own dishonesty. But the New Testament makes a claim that no human club ever makes about itself, that this people is the body of Christ on the earth, that he is the head and they are the limbs, that what is done to them is done to him. That is either delusion or revelation, but it is not a description of a club. A club you join for what it gives you and leave when it stops delivering. A body you are part of, and your leaving is not a cancelled membership but an amputation. The institution is real and often disappointing. The body is also real, and the disappointment does not unmake it, any more than a sick organ unmakes the body it belongs to.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If the church is a body and you are a member of it, what part have you gone numb to, the place where you have quietly told the rest of the body you have no need of it?
sessions.practice: This week, change one word in how you speak and think. Stop saying I am going to church and start saying I am gathering with the church, or simply we are the church. Each time you catch the old phrase, correct it, out loud if you can. Then notice, at the end of the week, whether the small change in language did anything to the way you see the people you gather with. Write down what shifted, even slightly.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, you did not save us into a private faith. You called us out of the world and into a people, a body, a household that is yours. Forgive us for shrinking the church down to a building we visit or a service we rate, and forgive us for the times we have stood apart and told the body we had no need of it. Teach us what it means to be members of one another, limbs of one body, dependent and joined. You who are the head, knit us back into the body you bled for. Amen.
reflection: When I am honest, do I treat the church as a people I belong to or as a service I attend and evaluate, and what does my answer reveal about what I think the church is?
Where have I told some part of the body, in word or in silence, that I have no need of it?
If the New Testament has no category for a solitary Christian, what would it mean for me to live as a member and not a spectator this week?
sessions.teaching: Start where Bell starts, with a man who loved Jesus and was finished with the church. He told Bell he could worship God just fine on his own, a Saturday morning, good coffee, an open Bible, no need for the building or the crowd or the disappointment. And Bell did not argue with him, because the man was not wrong about the disappointment. He asked him one question instead. Where, in the entire New Testament, do you find a single Christian living that way. The man could not name one, because there is not one. So we begin not with whether the church has failed us, which it has, plainly and often, but with the harder and prior question. What is the church. Because most of us are angry at, or bored by, or finished with a thing we have never once correctly named, and until we name it our grievance is aimed at the wrong target. Take the two pictures that quietly govern our imaginations, and take them at their strongest. The first says the church is a building. It is the place with the steeple, the address you drive to, the sanctuary you sit in. And this picture is not stupid, because the church does gather in places, and the gathering in a place is not nothing. The second picture says the church is an event, a service, the thing that happens for seventy-five minutes on a Sunday, the music and the talk and the lights and the feeling you either got or did not get. And this picture is not stupid either, because we do gather to worship, and what happens when the people of God assemble is not a small thing. But now watch what the New Testament does to both pictures, because it dismantles them without a word of argument, simply by never speaking the way we speak. The first Christians did not have buildings for nearly three centuries. The word translated church, ekklesia, never once in the New Testament means a building. It means an assembly, a people called out and gathered, the way a town crier would summon the citizens of a Greek city out of their houses into one body to decide the things that mattered. The church is the called-out ones. And the second picture falls just as fast, because Paul, when he reaches for the truest thing he can say about the church, does not call it a service or an event. He calls it a body. Now you are the body of Christ, he tells the Corinthians, and individually members of it. Sit with the weight of that word, member, because we have ruined it. We use member to mean someone with a card, a name on a roll, a person who has signed up for something. Paul does not mean that at all. He means a member the way a surgeon means it, a limb, a hand, a foot, an eye, an organ of a living body. A hand is not a hand because it filled out a form. It is a hand because it is attached to the arm, fed by the same blood, governed by the same head, dying the moment it is severed. That is what Paul says you are. Not a customer of the church. Not an attender of the church. A body part. And here is the verdict the whole session rests on, and the leader must hold it cleanly. This is why there is no solitary Christian in the New Testament, and the reason is not what we assume. It is not that solitary Christianity is forbidden, as though there were a rule against it that a brave or independent soul might break. It is that solitary Christianity is impossible, a contradiction in terms, like a severed hand that still expects to grip. The hand cannot say to the body, I have no need of you, and go on being a hand. It can only become a dead thing on the floor. When God saves you he does not merely fix your private account with heaven. He grafts you into a people. He makes you a living stone in a temple, a child in a household, a sheep in a flock, a limb in a body, and every one of those images is fatally communal. You cannot be a household of one. You cannot be a flock of one. You cannot be a body made of a single severed hand. And I have to stand inside this, because the consumer instinct is not only out in the pews, it has lived in me, in the pulpit. I have spent whole seasons treating the church as a service I produced rather than a people I belonged to, measuring a Sunday by whether it went well the way you measure a performance, thinking of the congregation as an audience to be moved rather than a body I was a limb of, bleeding and fed by the same blood. The diagnosis names the pastor before it names the man with the coffee and the Bible. So before we say one word about the marks of the church or its mess or its mission, we have to get the thing itself right. The church is not a building you visit. It is not an event you rate. It is the body of Christ, the called-out people of God, and you, if you are his, are not a guest of it. You are a part of it. And a part that imagines it can thrive cut off from the body has misunderstood what it is. Hear one more thing before we close, because it answers the man with the coffee and the Bible at the deepest level. He thought he was protecting something precious, his real faith, from the corruption of the institution. And his instinct was not entirely foolish, because the institution can corrupt and often does. But notice what the New Testament refuses to let him do. It will not let him have Christ without Christ's people, because Christ himself refuses to be had that way. When Saul was on the road to Damascus, persecuting the church, dragging Christians off to prison, the voice from heaven did not say why are you persecuting my followers. It said why are you persecuting me. Christ so identifies himself with his battered, imperfect, often embarrassing church that to touch them is to touch him, and to walk away from them is, in a way Saul never expected, to walk away from him. You cannot get to the head while despising the body, because the head will not be separated from the body he died to save. So when a person says I love Jesus but I am done with the church, the gentlest true thing you can say back is that Jesus is not done with the church, and he has tied himself to her so tightly that you cannot finally have the one without the other. The man wanted a clean Christ and a private faith. What the New Testament offers him is a crucified Christ who has made himself the head of a messy body and called that body his own, and bids the man come, not to a building and not to a service, but to a people, and be a part.

scriptureStudy.note: Now you are the body of Christ and individually members of it. Paul does not say the church is like a body. He says the church is the body, and you are an organ of it, which makes solitary Christianity as strange as a hand living apart from the arm.

The eye cannot say to the hand, I have no need of you. Paul forbids the very independence we prize, naming the conviction that I can do this alone as a kind of organ insisting it does not need the body, which is a sentence a body part cannot truthfully say.

You are members of the household of God, built into a holy temple, a dwelling place for God. Three communal images stacked together, household, temple, dwelling, none of which can be made of one person, all of which require being built in alongside others.

You yourselves like living stones are being built up as a spiritual house. A single stone is not a house, it is a stone in a field. Peter pictures each believer as a stone that means nothing structurally until it is set into the wall with the others.

They devoted themselves to the apostles teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers. The first picture of the church after Pentecost is not a building or a service but a devoted shared life, a people who could not be told apart from their life together.

On this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. Jesus is the one who promises to build the church, which means it is finally his project and his possession, not a human club we invented and may therefore dissolve.

Let us consider how to stir one another up, not neglecting to meet together, as is the habit of some. The command assumes a gathering and names the drifting away from it as a known danger, not a neutral lifestyle choice, because the stirring up cannot happen alone.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the long argument the church has had with itself about what makes the church the church, because the word ekklesia carries a history worth seeing. The first believers inherited the term from the Greek city, where the ekklesia was the assembly of citizens summoned out of their private affairs to gather as one body and act together, and from the Greek translation of the Old Testament, where the same word renders the assembly of Israel gathered before God at Sinai. Both backgrounds say the same thing. The church is a people called out and convened, never a place and never a private affair. Set that beside the modern Western drift, in which religion was quietly redefined as a private matter of personal belief, a thing between the individual and God that the institution merely services, and ask how much of our trouble with the church flows from this redefinition we have absorbed without noticing. A serious group should weigh the cost on both sides. The privatizing of faith has freed people from coercion and corrupt establishments, real goods worth keeping, and it has also produced a Christianity so individualized that the New Testament images of body and household and temple have become metaphors we admire rather than realities we inhabit. Read the older voices who could not conceive of a churchless Christian, weigh them against the genuine freedom of conscience the modern settlement won, and ask what it would mean to recover the communal substance of the faith without recovering the coercion. The discipline this whole study requires is to hold that the church is a people before it is anything else, that belonging to Christ and belonging to his body are not two decisions but one, and that the privatized faith so natural to us would have been unrecognizable to the people who first used the word church.
sessions.caseStudy: A woman in Bell's congregation, call her Marta, told him she had not missed a Sunday in eleven years and yet did not know a single person's last name. She arrived at the last possible minute, sat in the back, slipped out during the final song, and went home. She was, by every visible measure, a faithful churchgoer, and she was, by her own quiet admission, completely alone. When her husband left, no one in the church knew for three weeks, because there was no one positioned to know. Use Marta to test the difference between attending the church and being a member of the body. She had perfect attendance and no belonging. She was a hand that came to the building every week and never let itself be attached to the arm. Ask the group where they are like Marta, present and unjoined, and ask the harder question underneath it, what it would have cost her, and what it would cost them, to be known. Then ask what the body owed Marta, since a body that lets a member sit numb in the back for eleven years has also failed to be a body. The point cuts both ways. She would not be joined, and no one came to join her, and both are the failure the session is naming.

sessions.title: Life Together
sessions.aim: To follow Bonhoeffer into the difference between the Christian community we dream of and the one God actually gives, and to see that the death of our idealized fellowship is not the end of real fellowship but its doorway.
sessions.summary: Dietrich Bonhoeffer wrote a small book called Life Together out of an illegal seminary the Nazi state would soon shut down, a community of young pastors learning to live as the church under a regime that hated the church. The book contains one sentence that has wrecked more romantic notions of Christian community than any other. He who loves his dream of community more than the Christian community itself becomes a destroyer of that community. The first question is why our highest hopes for the church so often curdle into our deepest bitterness against it. Bell takes the strong form of the disillusioned, the person who came to the church starving for real fellowship and found gossip, cliques, and shallowness instead, and who is right to grieve it. He grants the grief its full weight. But Bonhoeffer names the hidden thing underneath the disappointment. We did not fall in love with the actual people God gave us. We fell in love with a picture of community in our own heads, an ideal, and when the real people failed to match the picture we blamed them for the gap. The dream becomes a measuring rod we beat the brothers and sisters with. Then the turn, and it is the strangest comfort in the study. Bonhoeffer says the disillusionment is a grace. The sooner the dream of an ideal community shatters, the better, because only when we stop demanding the church we imagined can we begin to receive the church God actually gave, made of forgiven sinners we did not choose, bound to us by Christ and not by our affinity. Real fellowship begins on the far side of disappointment, not before it.

keyScripture.why: Paul tells the Romans to welcome one another as Christ has welcomed them, grounding the acceptance of the actual, disappointing people in the room not in their meeting our standards but in the prior fact that Christ welcomed us while we fell short of his, which is the death of the idealized community and the birth of the real one.

discussion.q: Bonhoeffer says the person who loves his dream of community more than the actual community becomes its destroyer. Where have you loved your picture of what church should be more than the real people in front of you?
discussion.behind: Open on the central sentence of the session, and on self-recognition, not theory. Most of us carry an ideal of community and quietly resent the real one for failing it. The aim is to surface the dream itself, because we cannot repent of an idol we have not seen. Go first, and name your own dream honestly.

discussion.q: Think of a time the church disappointed you. Bell grants the disappointment is often justified. But how much of it was the church failing God, and how much was the church failing your picture of it?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves carefully. Some disappointment is righteous, the church really does fail God, and you must not dismiss real wounds as mere unmet preferences. The aim is the harder honesty of sorting the two, recognizing where our grievance is against sin and where it is against the gap between people and our ideal of them.

discussion.q: Bonhoeffer calls the shattering of our dream of community a grace. How can disillusionment with the church be a gift rather than simply a loss?
discussion.behind: This is the strange center of the session. We treat disillusionment as the end of fellowship, and Bonhoeffer treats it as the doorway. Help the room feel the paradox, that only when the ideal dies can we love the actual people, because the ideal was never going to let us love anyone real.

discussion.q: Paul says welcome one another as Christ welcomed you. Christ did not wait for you to meet his standard. What would it change to welcome the people in your church the way you were welcomed by Christ?
discussion.behind: Land the gospel ground under it. Our welcome of difficult people is meant to run on the same fuel as Christs welcome of us, which was not earned. Help the room see that the standard we hold others to is one we never met ourselves, and that grace received is the only thing that loosens the measuring rod.

discussion.q: Bell admits he has been more in love with the church he imagined leading than the church God actually gave him to love. Where do you love the church you wish you had more than the one you have?
discussion.behind: Close with self-implication, leader first. The dream of a better church is a quiet way of refusing the real one. Invite honest naming of the imagined better church we hold over the real one, and go first. The point is not guilt but the surrender of the ideal so the actual people become lovable.

objections.objection: But my disappointment with the church is not some idol in my head. The people really were shallow, the leaders really were proud, the community really was a letdown. You cannot just tell me my legitimate grievance is a dream I need to give up.
objections.response: Bell does not say that, and Bonhoeffer does not either, so hold this carefully. Some disappointment with the church is the perception of real sin, and that grief is righteous and must not be explained away as a personal preference, because to do so is its own cruelty to the wounded. The point is not that your grievance is imaginary. The point is the subtler thing underneath even legitimate grievance, the way we fuse our just complaint about real sin with our private picture of the ideal church, until we are no longer able to tell which is which, and the whole tangled mass becomes a reason to despise the actual people. Name the real sin, by all means, and call it what it is. But notice when the complaint has quietly become a refusal to love anyone who falls short of the community you imagined, because that one is not righteousness. That one is the dream turned into a weapon.

objections.objection: If I just accept the church as it is, dream and all dropped, am I not settling for mediocrity and giving up on the church ever being better than it is now?
objections.response: No, and Bonhoeffer is precise about this, so we should be too. Letting go of your idealized picture is not the same as abandoning all hope for the church to grow. It is the difference between two postures. One stands over the community as its judge, holding up a private blueprint and condemning everyone for the gap. The other stands inside the community as a forgiven member, loving the people as they are while praying and working for what they are not yet. The dream dropped is the judge stepping down off the bench. You do not stop longing for the church to be more like Christ. You stop making your own picture of perfection the condition on which you will deign to love the people. Real growth in a church almost never comes from the one demanding it from above. It comes from the one loving it from within.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What is the picture of the perfect church you have carried in your head, and who in your actual congregation have you quietly held in contempt for failing to be it?
sessions.practice: This week, pick one person in your church you find difficult, disappointing, or easy to dismiss, and do not avoid them. Instead, each day, pray for them by name, and ask God to show you one true thing to thank him for in them. Then, if you can, do one small act of welcome toward them, a conversation, a kindness, a refusal to write them off. Write down what it did to your heart toward them, and toward the church, by week's end.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, we came to your church carrying a picture of what it should be, and we have loved that picture more than the people you actually gave us. Forgive us for the contempt we have hidden under the name of high standards. You welcomed us while we fell far short of yours, and you ask us to welcome one another the same way. Let our dream of an ideal community die, all the way, so that we can finally love the real one, made of forgiven sinners we did not choose. Bind us to one another by Christ, and not by how well we measure up. Amen.
reflection: What does the church I dream of look like, and how have I used that dream as a measuring rod against the people God actually put in front of me?
Where is my disappointment with the church a grief over real sin, and where is it a grief that people are not the ideal I invented?
If Christ welcomed me before I met his standard, what is one relationship in the church where I have refused to extend the welcome I received?
sessions.teaching: Dietrich Bonhoeffer wrote a slim book called Life Together in the late nineteen thirties, and you have to know where it came from to feel its weight. He wrote it out of Finkenwalde, an underground seminary training pastors for the Confessing Church, the part of the German church that refused to bow to Hitler, and the Gestapo would shut it down within a couple of years. So this is not the reflection of a man romanticizing community from a comfortable distance. It is a man who lived in intense Christian fellowship under a regime that wanted that fellowship dead, writing down what he learned before the state scattered them, and before the state eventually hanged him. And in that book there is a sentence that has done more damage to our pretty notions of church than almost anything else ever written. He who loves his dream of community more than the Christian community itself becomes a destroyer of the latter, even though his personal intentions may be ever so honest and earnest and sacrificial. Read that twice, because it indicts the very people who care most. The first question we have to sit with is why our highest hopes for the church so reliably turn into our deepest bitterness toward it. Why is it that the people most wounded by the church are so often the ones who expected the most from it. Take the disillusioned person at full strength, because the grievance is usually real. Someone comes to the church starving, genuinely starving, for the kind of fellowship the New Testament describes, people who bear one anothers burdens, who know and are known, who love past the surface. And what they find instead is gossip in the parking lot, cliques that do not open, conversations that never go below the weather, leaders protecting their position, a coldness dressed up in warm language. That is a real disappointment, and it deserves to be grieved, and any pastor who waves it off as mere immaturity is part of the problem. Grant the grief its full weight. But now Bonhoeffer names the thing underneath the disappointment, and it is uncomfortable, because it turns the diagnosis back on us. We did not, most of us, fall in love with the actual flesh-and-blood people God placed in our church. We fell in love with a picture, an ideal of community we carried in our own heads, assembled from books and conferences and the best moments we ever experienced and a good deal of wishful thinking. And when the real people, the ones with bad breath and boring stories and irritating opinions and genuine sin, failed to match the picture, we did not blame our picture. We blamed them. The ideal became a measuring rod, and we beat the brothers and sisters with it, often while congratulating ourselves on having such high standards for the body of Christ. This is the trap. The dream of community, Bonhoeffer says, can be the very thing that makes real community impossible, because the dreamer is so busy loving the church in his head that he never gets around to loving the church in the room. And here is where it turns, and the turn is the strangest comfort in this whole study. Bonhoeffer says that the disillusionment, the shattering of the dream, is a grace. He writes that the sooner this shock of disillusionment comes to an individual and to a community the better for both. Sit with how counterintuitive that is. We treat disillusionment as the death of fellowship, the moment we discover the church is not what we hoped and start edging toward the door. Bonhoeffer treats it as the doorway. Because only when the ideal community dies, only when we stop demanding that the church match our picture, can we begin to receive and love the church God actually gave us, which is the only one that exists. The community made of forgiven sinners we did not choose and would not have chosen, bound to us not by natural affinity or shared taste but by Jesus Christ alone. That is the foundation Bonhoeffer keeps returning to. Christian community is not an ideal we realize. It is a reality created by God in Christ in which we participate. We are not joined to these people because they are wonderful or because we picked them. We are joined to them because Christ joined himself to all of us, and Paul puts the whole thing on exactly that ground. Welcome one another, he tells the Romans, as Christ has welcomed you. Stop right there. How did Christ welcome you. Not after you cleaned up. Not once you met his standard. Not when you became the ideal disciple he was hoping for. He welcomed you in the middle of your sin, while you were still his enemy, falling laughably short of his glory, and that unearned welcome is the exact pattern and the exact fuel for how we are to welcome the difficult, disappointing, ordinary people in our pews. The standard we hold them to is one we never met. And I have to put myself in the center of this, because it is the pastors temptation in its purest form. I have been more in love with the church I imagined leading than the church God actually handed me to love. I have stood in front of the real congregation, the actual people, and felt a low disappointment that they were not the people in my head, the more responsive, more committed, more interesting congregation of my imagination, and that disappointment is not high standards. It is the dream turned into contempt, and it makes me, in Bonhoeffers terrible phrase, a destroyer of the very community I was ordained to serve. So let the dream die. Let it shatter all the way, the picture of the perfect church and the perfect small group and the perfect Christian friends, because that picture has been standing between you and the people Christ actually bled for and actually placed beside you. Real fellowship does not live before the disappointment. It lives on the far side of it, where you have stopped loving your idea of the church and started loving the church, the only one there is, the one God gave.

scriptureStudy.note: Welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God. The standard for accepting difficult people is not whether they meet our ideal but how Christ accepted us, which was before we met his, dismantling the measuring rod entirely.

With all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love. Paul assumes there will be much to bear with, building the patience for one anothers faults into the job description of belonging, not treating it as a sign the community has failed.

Bearing with one another and, if one has a complaint against another, forgiving each other, as the Lord has forgiven you. The forgiving is constant and mutual, grounded again in the forgiveness we received, which is the only thing strong enough to absorb the friction of real community.

If anyone says I love God and hates his brother, he is a liar. John forbids the very split the dreamer attempts, loving God and the ideal church while despising the actual brother in front of him, naming it not as high standards but as a lie.

By this all people will know you are my disciples, if you have love for one another. The mark of the church before the world is not its excellence or its programs but the love among ordinary members, which can only exist once the demand for an ideal community is laid down.

Love is patient and kind, it is not irritable or resentful, it bears all things. Paul describes love as precisely the opposite of the dreamers contempt, patient with the real and unirritated by the gap between people and the ideal.

In humility count others more significant than yourselves, looking to their interests. The dreamer counts the community significant only as it serves his picture, while Paul commands the reverse, a regard for the actual others that the idealized vision can never produce.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up Bonhoeffers larger argument in Life Together, because the famous line about the dream of community sits inside a whole theology of fellowship worth weighing. Bonhoeffer insists that Christian community is mediated, that we do not come to one another directly but always through Christ, and that this is not a limitation but the only thing that makes durable community possible. Where human fellowship runs on attraction and affinity, on liking the same things and being the same kind of person, Christian fellowship runs on the fact that Christ stands between every two believers and binds them in himself, which means it can hold people together who would never have chosen each other and would not survive the disappointments of direct, unmediated relationship. Set this beside the modern friendship economy, in which we curate our relationships by preference, sorting ourselves into communities of the like-minded and quietly dropping anyone who no longer fits, and ask what is lost when the church becomes one more affinity group selected by taste. A serious group should weigh both the promise and the danger here. The promise is a community that can include the person you would never have befriended, which is the only kind that looks anything like the kingdom. The danger is using mediated community as an excuse to avoid the ordinary human work of actually knowing and liking and being present to one another, hiding behind Christ-between-us to keep a safe distance. The discipline Bonhoeffer presses is to receive the people God gives rather than the people we would assemble, to let Christ be the bond rather than our compatibility, and to discover that the community we did not design is finally deeper than the one we would have, because it is built on something sturdier than our shifting preferences.
sessions.caseStudy: A young couple, new believers, joined a small group expecting the kind of fellowship they had read about in Acts, lives shared, burdens carried, a found family. Within four months they were gone, and on the way out the husband told Bell the group was shallow and cliquey and not real community. He was partly right. The group was awkward and uneven, the conversations sometimes thin, two of the members genuinely hard to like. But Bell had also watched this couple, and what he saw was a pair of people measuring every gathering against a picture in their heads and finding each one wanting, never staying in any group long enough to become the depth they were demanding from it. Use them to work Bonhoeffer's line in real time. They loved their dream of community so much that they could not love the actual people long enough for community to form, and so they became, in the small way the line predicts, destroyers of the very thing they wanted, leaving a group slightly more discouraged each time. Ask the group whether the couple's complaint was about real shallowness or about the gap between people and an ideal, and press the harder point, that the depth they wanted only ever grows on the far side of staying through the disappointment they kept refusing to stay through.

sessions.title: The Marks and the Mess
sessions.aim: To hold together two things the church keeps trying to pull apart, the marks that make a true church and the mess that fills every real one, so that the room can take the scandal of a divided and hypocritical church seriously without using it as a reason to walk away from a hospital they still need.
sessions.summary: The Reformers, sorting out which gatherings were truly the church and which were not, settled on simple marks. Where the Word of God is rightly preached, the sacraments rightly administered, and discipline practiced, there is a true church, however poor and small. The first question is why a study that has talked about the body and about life together suddenly needs marks at all, fences around the thing. Bell takes the strong form of the cynic who says the marks are just gatekeeping, a way for the religious to decide who counts, and a way to pretend the church is purer than it is. He grants real weight to the suspicion, because the marks have been abused exactly that way. But the marks are not a purity test. They are the church saying what it actually is for. Word, so that Christ is heard and not merely the pastors opinions. Sacrament, the bread and the water that preach with their substance what words alone cannot. Discipline, not to expel the sinful, since the church is nothing but sinners, but to keep the body honest about sin rather than baptizing it. And then the mess, taken head on. The church is a hospital for sinners, not a museum for saints, which means a healthy church will always look more like an emergency room than a gallery, full of the wounded and the contagious and the not-yet-well. The scandal is real, the divisions and the hypocrisy and the covered-up sin, and Bell refuses to minimize any of it. But a sick body is still a body, and a hospital full of sick people is not an argument against hospitals. It is the reason they exist.

keyScripture.why: Jesus says those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick, and that he came not to call the righteous but sinners, defining the church he is building as a gathering of the sick under treatment rather than a display of the already healthy, which reframes the messiness of the church as exactly what we should expect to find.

discussion.q: The old marks of a true church are Word, sacrament, and discipline. Before tonight, if someone asked you what makes a gathering actually a church and not just a religious club, what would you have said?
discussion.behind: Surface the working definition of a true church. Most people answer with vibe, size, music, or friendliness, which exposes how far our instincts have drifted from the marks. The aim is not to shame the answers but to notice what we have been measuring the church by, so the marks can reframe it. Go first if the room is slow.

discussion.q: Bell takes seriously the suspicion that marks and discipline are just gatekeeping, the religious deciding who counts. What is true in that worry, and how is the actual purpose of the marks different?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves. The marks have been abused as purity tests and weapons, and the cynic is right to have seen it. The difference is that the marks describe what the church is for, Christ heard, the gospel made visible, sin kept honest, not a fence to keep people out. Help the room separate the abuse from the thing abused.

discussion.q: Bell says the church is a hospital for sinners, not a museum for saints. How does it change your expectations of the church to picture an emergency room full of the sick rather than a gallery of the already well?
discussion.behind: Land the central image. We come to church braced to find saints and feel betrayed by the sin, or we come hiding our own sickness to fit in among the well. The aim is to reset the expectation, so that finding the church full of struggling sinners, ourselves included, stops being a scandal and starts being the point.

discussion.q: The hypocrisy and division of the church is a real scandal, and Bell refuses to minimize it. Where has the failure of the church most damaged your trust, and what do you do with that wound?
discussion.behind: Make room for real wounds without rushing to defend the church. Some in the room carry deep injuries from church failure and need them named, not explained away. The aim is honest grief first. Only after the wound is honored can the room consider whether a sick hospital is still worth needing.

discussion.q: Bell admits he has, as a pastor, helped the church look more like a museum than a hospital, polishing an image instead of treating the sick. Where have you helped your church perform health it did not have?
discussion.behind: Close with self-implication, leader first. We all collude in the museum, hiding our own sickness and rewarding others for hiding theirs. Invite honest naming of the ways we perform wellness, and go first. The point is not guilt but the recovery of a church honest enough to be a hospital.

objections.objection: The church is full of hypocrites. People who say one thing on Sunday and live another all week, leaders who covered up abuse, Christians more political than Christlike. Why would I belong to an institution that rotten?
objections.response: Do not rush to defend, because much of this is simply true, and the wound behind it is often real. The church has harbored hypocrites, covered up genuine evil, traded Jesus for power and partisanship, and any honest pastor has to say so plainly and grieve it rather than minimize it. Sit with that fully. Then offer the reframing without using it to dodge the sin. A hospital full of sick people is not an argument against hospitals, it is what a hospital is. If the church is, as Jesus says, a gathering of the sick under the care of a physician, then finding it full of sinners is not a scandal that disproves it, it is the very thing it claims to be. The real scandal is not that the church is full of hypocrites. It is when the church pretends it is not, when it becomes a museum performing a health it does not have. The honest sinner church, the one that admits its sickness and submits to the physician, is the credible one. And yes, you are one of the sick. So am I. The hospital was never for the well.

objections.objection: If the church is just a hospital of sinners and everyone is a mess, then does sin even matter? Why have discipline at all? It sounds like a license to do whatever you want as long as you show up.
objections.response: No, and this is exactly why the third mark exists, so hold it carefully. A hospital that never treated the sickness, that just gathered sick people and told them their disease did not matter, would not be a hospital. It would be a hospice pretending to be a clinic. Discipline is the church taking sin seriously precisely because it loves the sinner, the way a doctor takes the tumor seriously. It is not about expelling the flawed, since the church is nothing but the flawed, and a church that disciplined everyone for being a sinner would empty in an hour. It is about refusing to call the sickness health, refusing to baptize the sin, walking with the sinner toward repentance rather than leaving them to die comfortable. Grace is not the absence of truth about sin. It is the love that names the sin in order to heal it. A hospital that lied about your diagnosis would not be kind. It would be killing you politely.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What sickness in your own life have you been hiding in church, performing wellness on Sunday while the disease goes untreated because you are afraid the hospital is actually a museum?
sessions.practice: This week, do one honest thing to treat the church as a hospital rather than a museum. Tell one trusted person in your church one true thing about how you are actually doing, not the Sunday answer. Or, if you are the one who has been judging the sick around you, pick one person you have written off as a hypocrite and ask God to let you see them as a fellow patient instead. Write down what it cost you, and what it opened.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord Jesus, you said you came not for the well but for the sick, not to call the righteous but sinners, and that means you came for a church exactly like ours, full of the wounded and the contagious and the not-yet-healed. Forgive us for turning your hospital into a museum, for performing a health we do not have and despising the sick who could not perform it. We grieve the real evil the church has done and hidden, and we ask you to heal what it has broken. Keep us honest about our sickness and submitted to you, the physician. Do not let us leave the hospital because it is full of the sick. Amen.
reflection: When I look at the church, do I expect a museum of saints and feel betrayed by the sin, or do I expect a hospital of sinners and find that I am one of the patients?
Where has the real hypocrisy and failure of the church wounded me, and have I let that wound harden into a reason to refuse the help I still need?
What sickness have I been hiding rather than bringing to the physician, and who in the body could I finally be honest with?
sessions.teaching: When the Reformers in the sixteenth century had to answer a hard question, they gave a surprisingly simple answer. The question was this. With the church split and competing bodies each claiming to be the true one, how do you tell a real church from a counterfeit. And they did not answer with size, or beauty, or the holiness of the members, or how good it made you feel. They answered with marks, notae, signs you could actually look for. Wherever the Word of God is purely preached and heard, and the sacraments administered according to Christs institution, there, they said, a church of God exists, however small and poor it may be. Many added a third mark, the practice of discipline. So the first honest question is why a study that has spent two sessions on the body and on life together suddenly needs marks at all, fences and tests, which feel like the opposite of the warmth we have been describing. Take the cynics objection at full strength, because it has teeth. The cynic says the marks are gatekeeping, a way for the religious to draw a line and decide who is in and who is out, and worse, a way to pretend the church is purer and more defined than the messy reality ever is. And the cynic is not making this up, because the marks have in fact been wielded exactly that way, as weapons, as purity tests, as instruments of exclusion by people who wanted a tidy church and a clear enemy. Grant all of that. But the marks, rightly understood, are not a purity test at all. They are the church saying out loud what it is actually for, what makes it the church and not merely a club with religious decor. Consider them quickly. The first mark is the Word rightly preached, which means that in a true church you encounter Christ speaking through the Scriptures, not merely the pastors opinions or the spirit of the age in a nice suit. A gathering where the Word is not truly preached may have lights and crowds and feeling, but the living voice of God is not in it, and that absence is fatal. The second mark is the sacraments, baptism and the Lords Supper, the water and the bread and the cup, and these matter because they preach with their substance what words alone cannot. The bread broken says the body broken. The cup poured says the blood poured out. They are the gospel you can taste and feel and be washed in, given to a people too prone to reduce faith to ideas. The third mark, discipline, is the one we flinch at, and we will come back to it, but its purpose is not to expel the sinful, which would be absurd, since the church is nothing but the sinful. Its purpose is to keep the body honest about sin instead of baptizing it. Now hold the marks in one hand and pick up the mess with the other, because here is where the session has to be brave. The church is, as the old line has it, a hospital for sinners and not a museum for saints. And that single image, if you let it land, reorganizes everything. We walk into church carrying one of two false expectations. Either we expect a museum, a gallery of the already holy, polished saints behind velvet ropes, and then we are scandalized and embittered when we find the gossip and the pride and the covered-up sin, as though we had been promised a gallery and handed a ward. Or we come hiding our own sickness, performing wellness, terrified that everyone else is well and we are the only one bleeding, so we never get treated at all. Jesus blows up both. They who are well, he says, have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners. That is the church he is building, on purpose. A gathering of the sick under the care of the physician. So when you walk into a church and find it full of sinners, including some appalling ones, you have not discovered a scandal that disproves the church. You have discovered exactly what it claims to be. The emergency room is full of the bleeding because that is what an emergency room is for. A hospital crowded with sick people is not an argument against hospitals. Now I have to be honest about the scandal, because the reframing can be misused as a dodge, and I will not let it be. The hypocrisy of the church is real. The divisions are real, thousands of them, a body hacked into competing pieces, often over pride dressed as principle. The covered-up abuse is real and damnable, the worst of it done by people protecting the institution while sacrificing the sheep. The marriage of the church to political power and cultural grievance is real, and it has made the name of Christ a stench to people he died for. None of that is excused by the hospital image, and a pastor who uses hospital for sinners to wave away genuine evil is committing a second sin on top of the first. The hospital is not an excuse for the disease. It is the place the disease is supposed to be treated, named, fought, not hidden and not celebrated. Which is exactly why the third mark, discipline, is not cruelty but love. A hospital that gathered the sick and then told them the cancer did not matter, that refused ever to name a disease or apply a treatment, would not be merciful. It would be killing people politely while they thanked it for being so accepting. Discipline is the church refusing to lie about your diagnosis. It is not about throwing out the flawed, since that would empty every pew including the pulpit. It is about walking the sinner toward repentance and health rather than leaving him comfortable in what is killing him, and it is meant to be done with the gentleness of someone who knows he is a patient too. And here I am implicated as deeply as anyone, because the temptation of the pastor is to run a museum. I have helped the church perform a health it did not have, curated an image of a put-together congregation, rewarded the people who hid their sickness well and quietly found the visibly broken ones inconvenient, because a hospital is messier and harder to advertise than a gallery. That is its own hypocrisy, and it is mine. So here is the verdict, and the leader should hold it steadily through the wounds in the room. The church has the marks and the church has the mess, and you cannot have one without the other this side of heaven. A true church is not a clean one. It is one where the Word is preached, the sacraments given, and sin treated rather than hidden, and it will, every time, look more like a crowded emergency room than a quiet museum. The sin in the church is not finally a reason to leave the hospital. It is, if you are honest about your own diagnosis, the reason you needed it in the first place.

scriptureStudy.note: Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. Jesus defines his mission and his church around the sick, so a church full of sinners is not a failure of the project but the project itself, the hospital doing what hospitals do.

Preach the word, be ready in season and out of season. The first mark, the Word rightly preached, is a charge so that the living voice of Christ is heard in the church and not merely human opinion dressed in religious clothes.

As often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lords death until he comes. The sacrament preaches by its substance, the broken bread and poured cup announcing the gospel to a people who would otherwise reduce faith to ideas.

If your brother sins against you, go and tell him his fault between you and him alone. Jesus gives the pattern of discipline as a careful, escalating pursuit of the sinner aimed at winning him back, not at expelling him, a treatment and not a purge.

If anyone is caught in any transgression, restore him in a spirit of gentleness, keeping watch on yourself. Restoration is the goal of discipline and gentleness its manner, with the warning that the one doing it is a fellow patient who could be next.

Is Christ divided. Paul grieves the factions in Corinth, naming division as a scandal against the one body, which honors the real wound of a fractured church without ever suggesting the answer is to abandon it.

If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, but if we confess our sins he is faithful to forgive. John makes confession, not pretended wellness, the way of life in the church, the difference between an honest hospital and a lying museum.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the old distinction between the visible and the invisible church, because it is the tool the tradition forged to hold exactly the tension this session lives in. The invisible church is the whole company of the truly redeemed, known finally only to God, the people who are actually in Christ. The visible church is the church you can see and join and be hurt by, the mixed body of true believers and hypocrites and the not-yet-converted, all gathered under the same roof, indistinguishable from the outside and often from the inside. Augustine, arguing against the Donatists who wanted a pure church of only the holy, insisted that the wheat and the weeds grow together until the harvest and that no human hand should try to sort them early, because the attempt to purify the church of all sinners always ends in either delusion or tyranny. Set this beside the recurring modern impulse to find or found the real church, the pure one, the one without the hypocrisy and the institutional rot, an impulse that drives both the restless church-hopper and the disillusioned exile, and ask what the Donatist error teaches about where that impulse leads. A serious group should weigh the danger on both sides. The Donatist longing for purity contains a real good, the hunger for a holy church that does not lie about sin, and it curdles into a cruelty that would uproot the wheat with the weeds and leave a church of one. The opposite error, a lazy tolerance that calls every weed wheat and abandons the marks altogether, is just as deadly. The discipline the tradition presses is to belong to the visible church honestly, knowing it is mixed and messy and not yet the spotless bride, while trusting that Christ is even now at work purifying it for the day it will be, and refusing both the fantasy of a pure church now and the surrender that stops longing for purity at all.
sessions.caseStudy: A man Bell calls Dean had been an elder for two decades, respected, quoted, the one people pointed to as a pillar. When his hidden addiction finally surfaced, the church split clean down the middle. Half wanted him gone immediately, the hypocrite exposed, the museum scandalized that one of its statues had a crack. The other half wanted the whole thing buried, no consequences, because Dean was important and the church's reputation was at stake, the institution protecting its image. Almost no one in either camp wanted what discipline actually is, which is the slow, painful, loving work of naming the sin truthfully and walking Dean toward repentance and health without either expelling him or pretending the sickness was fine. Use Dean to show the room both failures of a church around sin, the purge that treats a sinner as garbage and the cover-up that treats sin as nothing, and to recover the third way the marks describe. Ask which instinct they feel first when a respected person falls, the urge to expel or the urge to protect the image, and ask what it would have looked like to treat Dean as a patient with a serious disease rather than as either a criminal to discard or a secret to hide.
